content.text: Students build from source credibility and usefulness work to decide which sources most directly help answer their research question.
Research becomes more accurate and complete when students prioritize the evidence that most directly answers important questions.
Students will paraphrase from their top sources, organize notes by category, and begin drafting clear explanations of contribution and impact.
Today’s work helps students choose the strongest evidence base for their final informational research writing, argument paragraph, and presentation visuals.

Directions:

Yesterday, we figured out which sources were most useful for our research. Today, we are taking that a step further by deciding which sources most directly answer our inquiry questions. Think-pair-share with a classmate about the following question:
How is a relevant source different from a source that is only generally related to your topic?

Researchers do not just collect information—they test whether that information actually answers their question. One way to do that is by paraphrasing. When I restate a detail in my own words, I can see more clearly whether it is

, or if it is just general background.
Model Sentence
The engineer tested the heat shield many times and showed that it protected the capsule during reentry.
Directions:
Choose one short sentence from one of your sources.
Paraphrase the sentence in your own words.
Then answer:
Does this detail directly answer your inquiry question?
Is it central evidence or background information?
Part A: Which Sources Answer the Question
Relevant sources do at least one of these jobs:
directly explain the innovator’s key contribution
provide evidence about impact, obstacles, or recognition
answer a specific inquiry question with details
include supporting visuals or features that clarify important information
Think-Pair-Share
Directions:

Choose three sources from your current set. For each source, find one detail that directly relates to your research topic and one detail that is less central. Then rank the sources from most relevant to least relevant for your research right now.
With a partner, discuss your findings and answer the question.
Which source most directly answers your inquiry question, and what specific detail makes it the most relevant?
Part B: Build Your Final Short List
Directions:
Build your final list of sources to answer your research question.

Review your ranked sources. Choose the two to three sources that are both most relevant and most useful for your inquiry questions. Write those source titles in the left column of the middle rows of your Research Notes graphic organizer.
Check for Understanding
Reflect on your ability to identify relevant sources using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in identifying the most relevant sources for your inquiry questions?
Quick Write
Directions:
In two to three sentences, name your most relevant source and explain why it belongs at the top of your list. Compare it to one less central source and explain what makes the difference.

This section helps students refine their research decision-making by distinguishing between sources that are generally related to a topic and those that directly answer an inquiry question. Students build on prior work with credibility and usefulness to develop a clearer understanding of relevance as the most important factor in selecting evidence for research. Emphasize that strong researchers prioritize sources that provide specific, direct information about an innovator’s contribution, impact, or recognition rather than sources that only offer background or broad context. Students should begin to recognize that relevance determines which sources will actually support their final writing and presentation tasks. Students also continue applying media analysis skills by deciding whether sections, headings, captions, diagrams, or timelines provide central evidence or only extra background information.
Have students take out their sources from previous lessons and their Research Notes graphic organizer.
Think-Pair-Share
Say these Directions:

Yesterday, we figured out which sources were most useful for our research. Today, we are taking that a step further by deciding which sources most directly answer our inquiry questions. Think-pair-share with a classmate about the following question:
Ask:
How is a relevant source different from a source that is only generally related to your topic?

A relevant source directly answers my inquiry question or explains my innovator’s key contribution. A source that is only generally related may mention the person or topic, but it does not give the information I need most for my research.
Teacher Tip
Use this routine to connect yesterday’s work on usefulness to today’s work on relevance. The goal is to move students from broad source selection to evidence hierarchy.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that we can name the difference between related information and relevant evidence, let’s test which sources truly belong in our research set.
Students will activate prior learning about credibility and usefulness and connect it to today’s task of deciding which sources most directly answer a research question.
Paraphrasing to Evaluate Relevance

Use this routine to teach students how to paraphrase source information in order to determine whether it is specific and direct enough to support their inquiry question. Students learn that paraphrasing is not just a writing skill—it helps researchers decide if a source provides usable evidence or only general background information.
Say:

Researchers do not just collect information—they test whether that information actually answers their question. One way to do that is by paraphrasing. When I restate a detail in my own words, I can see more clearly whether it is specific, direct, and
useful, or if it is just general background.
Model Sentence
The engineer tested the heat shield many times and showed that it protected the capsule during reentry.
Explain that paraphrasing does not mean changing one or two words. It means keeping the original meaning while rebuilding the sentence in a new way.
Say:

First, I ask, “What is the key idea?” The key idea is that repeated testing proved the heat shield protected the capsule. Now I can paraphrase: “Repeated testing provided evidence of the heat shield’s effectiveness, particularly in protecting the capsule during reentry.”
Say:

Finally I ask: Does this detail directly answer my research question, or is it just background? This detail is relevant because it explains the innovator’s contribution, the heat shield, and why it mattered, it protected the capsule.
Student Task
Now students practice the skill, using their own sources collected for their chosen subject.
Say these Directions:
Choose one short sentence from one of your sources.
Paraphrase the sentence in your own words.
Then answer:
Does this detail directly answer your inquiry question?
Is it central evidence or background information?
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
When you paraphrase clearly, you can make stronger decisions about which sources—and which details—belong in your research. Next, you will use this same thinking to rank your sources by relevance.
Students learn to restate technical information in their own words so they can take usable research notes without plagiarizing.
Language Focus:
Nominalization with academic nouns such as contribution, protection, testing, recognition
Precision language such as “largely due to,” “as a result of,” “because of”
Formal claim language such as “provided evidence,” “demonstrated,” “showed the significance of”
Before Sentence Expansion (preparation step—optional)
Students underline one action word in the source sentence and orally say the noun form before they write.
Prompt students to name the key idea first so they paraphrase meaning, not just vocabulary.
Encourage students to keep necessary technical terms but change the sentence structure and most of the surrounding wording.
You said "It worked because they tested it a lot"—we can say: "Repeated testing provided evidence of its effectiveness."
You said "This mattered because it kept the capsule safe"—we can say: "Its significance came largely from its protection of the capsule during reentry."
The source explains ___, so my paraphrase is ___.
The significance of this detail comes largely due to ___.
___ was important because it provided evidence of ___.
Invite students to orally rehearse the idea in everyday language first, including with a partner who shares a home language, and then move it into formal academic English.
Encourage students to connect nominalizations they notice in English to similar noun forms they know in other languages.
If students copy most of the source sentence and swap only one or two words → Prompt: "Cover the source and say the main idea aloud in your own words before you write again."
If students remove the science meaning while trying to sound formal → Prompt: "Keep the technical term if you need it, but rebuild the rest of the sentence around the idea."
If students write a fact without explaining why it matters → Prompt: "Add a precise phrase like 'largely due to' or 'as a result of' to show significance."
Student restates a source detail in new wording while keeping the original meaning accurate.
Student uses at least one nominalization or precise explanation phrase to make the paraphrase more formal and useful for research notes.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Avoiding Plagiarism
Have students cover the source after reading it once, say the main idea aloud, and then write from memory before checking the original.
Nominalization: Offer a quick oral model. Ex. Test becomes testing, protect becomes protection, contribute becomes contribution.
Precise Explanation Language: Provide a short bank of phrases students can reuse: largely due to, as a result of, because of, which shows the significance of.
Written Expression: Allow students to record their paraphrase orally first or use speech-to-text before writing the final version in their journal.
Ready for extension
Deepen the Paraphrase: Invite students to write a second version that combines two related details from the same source into one formal academic claim.
Strengthen Precision: Ask students to explain how their paraphrase highlights the innovator’s contribution, impact, or recognition more clearly than the original wording.
Students will paraphrase key details from sources in order to determine whether the information is specific and direct enough to support their research question.
Part A: Which Sources Answer the Question (W.6.8) (15 minutes)

This section focuses on helping students evaluate how directly a source answers their inquiry question by identifying central versus less relevant details. Students learn to prioritize evidence by examining whether a source explains the innovator’s key contribution, provides specific supporting details, or includes meaningful visuals that clarify understanding. Emphasize that relevance is determined by how clearly and directly a source contributes to answering the research question, not simply by whether it mentions the topic. Students should begin ranking sources using evidence-based reasoning, preparing them to build a focused and effective research set.
Say these Directions:
Relevant sources do at least one of these jobs:
directly explain the innovator’s key contribution
provide evidence about impact, obstacles, or recognition
answer a specific inquiry question with details
include supporting visuals or features that clarify important information
Explain that less relevant sources may still mention the topic but stay too broad, repeat known facts, or focus on side issues.
Teacher Think-Aloud:
Say:

I am looking at three sources, and they all connect to my innovator in some way. One source gives a general biography, one source explains the actual scientific work, and one source focuses mostly on the history of NASA. The NASA history source is interesting and related, but it is not directly answering my question about the innovator’s contribution. In the section with the labeled diagram, the second source specifically explains the work and its effect, so it is more relevant. That is the kind of source I want to keep.
Think-Pair-Share
Say these Directions:

Choose three sources from your current set. For each source, find one detail that directly relates to your research topic and one detail that is less central. Then rank the sources from most relevant to least relevant for your research right now.
With a partner, discuss your findings and answer the question.
Ask:
Which source most directly answers your inquiry question, and what specific detail makes it the most relevant?

The science article is the most relevant because, in the section explaining the innovator’s experiment, it directly shows what the contribution was and why it changed the field. The biography source mentions the person’s life, but it does not specifically address the key contribution in as much detail.

This section builds students’ ability to prioritize sources by distinguishing between central evidence and less relevant details. Students should be able to explain why one source ranks higher than another by pointing to specific sections, features, or information that directly answer their inquiry question. Emphasize that strong researchers justify rankings using clear evidence rather than general impressions. By the end of this section, students should be able to identify the most relevant source and defend that choice using precise academic language.
Students identify which evidence directly answers their inquiry questions and justify a relevance ranking using precise language.
Language Focus:
Prioritization language including “most relevant,” “less central,” “key contribution”
Direct relation language including “directly answers,” “specifically addresses”
Comparison and contrast structures with while, however, and compared to
Before Think-Pair-Share (Preparation Step—Optional)
Students silently reread one inquiry question and one section of a source that seems to answer it most directly.
Push students to identify exact details rather than broad summaries.
Encourage students to separate central evidence from background information.
This source is most relevant because it directly answers ___.
Compared to the other source, this one specifically addresses ___.
While this source provides background, this other source explains the key contribution.
If students rank a source without evidence → Prompt: “Point to the section, heading, or detail that proves why it belongs higher or lower.”
If students treat all details as equally important → Prompt: “Ask which detail you would actually use to answer your inquiry question in writing.”
If students rely on vague words like important → Prompt: “Replace important with relevant, central, or directly related.”
Student names a specific inquiry question when ranking a source.
Student distinguishes a central detail from a less relevant detail.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Determining Direct Connection
Prompt students to finish
Ex. This source answers my question about ___ because ___.
Struggling with: Filtering Unrelated Information
Ask: Which detail would you skip if you only had room for one strongest piece of evidence?
Struggling with: Academic Precision
Offer a short word bank with relevant, central, specific, direct, background, and side detail.
Struggling with: Alternative Expression
Allow students to explain one relevance ranking orally before writing it on the organizer.
Ready for extension: Include Lower-Ranked Sources
Ask students to add a note explaining whether a lower-ranked source should still be kept for background, obstacles, or recognition.
Part B: Build Your Final Short List (W.6.7) (15 minutes)

This section guides students in narrowing their research to a small set of highly relevant and useful sources that will form the foundation of their final work. Students apply their understanding of relevance to select only those sources that most directly support their inquiry questions and provide strong evidence for explaining an innovator’s contribution and impact. Emphasize that effective researchers do not keep every source they find but instead curate a focused set of materials that will lead to clearer, more accurate writing. Students should begin to see how selecting stronger sources now will make note-taking, paraphrasing, and drafting more efficient and meaningful in upcoming lessons.
Say:
Researchers need a short list of sources that are both
useful
and
relevant

. Usefulness tells us if a source has helpful information. A source can be useful, but not relevant enough to include in our final list. Relevance answers this question: Which sources most directly help me explain my innovator’s contribution and significance? You will record your two to three most relevant and useful sources in your
Research Notes
graphic organizer.
Say:

I do not need every source I found. I only need the sources that most directly help me explain the innovator’s work and why it matters. One source gives great background information, but another source is more relevant because, in the section under the heading about the discovery, it specifically addresses my inquiry question. While both sources relate to my topic, the second source belongs in my top list because it will give me stronger notes for writing. That is the source I will record first in my Research Notes organizer.
Say these Directions:

Review your ranked sources. Choose the two to three sources that are both most relevant and most useful for your inquiry questions. Write those source titles in the left column of the middle rows of your
Research Notes
graphic organizer.
Ask:
Which source will you record first in your Research Notes organizer, and why is it central to your research?

I will record the museum article first because it directly explains my innovator’s key contribution and includes a diagram that makes the process easier to understand. While another source gives broader background, this source is more relevant because it specifically addresses the question I need to answer in my final project.

By the end of this section, students should be able to justify why a source is central by referencing how it directly answers their inquiry question or explains a key contribution. Emphasize that selecting stronger sources strengthens the quality of their final writing and reduces reliance on less useful background information.
Students finalize a short list of sources and explain why one source is central to their research plan.
Language Focus:
Prioritization language including “central to,” “most relevant,” “top source”
Concessive clauses including “while this relates”
Precision language including “specifically addresses,” “directly relates,” “key contribution”
Academic nouns including relevance, recognition, visibility, representation
Students orally rehearse one sentence beginning “This source is central to my research because ___.”
Prompt students to record only the sources they are most likely to use for notes and writing.
Encourage students to explain relevance with evidence from the source, not only with general praise.
This source directly relates to my inquiry because ___.
While this source relates to ___, it is less central because ___.
This source is central to my research because it explains the innovator’s key contribution.
If students choose too many sources → Prompt: “Which two or three sources would you keep if you had to begin note-taking today?”
If students justify with vague statements like “It has good information” → Prompt: “Name the exact question, contribution, or detail the source helps explain.”
If students confuse general topic connection with relevance → Prompt: “Ask whether the source directly answers the inquiry or only mentions the topic.”
Student records two or three source titles in the correct place on the Research Notes organizer.
Student writes an explanation that names why one source is central to the inquiry.
Connection to Today's Learning
Students now have a clearer evidence hierarchy and a stronger Research Notes organizer. In the next lesson, they will begin paraphrasing and recording key information from these top sources.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Recording the Correct Sources
Direct students to star their top two or three on the ranking organizer before copying them into the Research Notes graphic organizer.
Struggling with: Explaining Centrality
Provide a sentence frame. Ex. This source is central to my research because it directly answers ___.
Struggling with: Academic Phrasing
Invite students to replace “talks about” with “specifically addresses” or “directly relates to.”
Struggling with: Alternative Expression
Allow students to explain why a source is central orally before writing their final sentence.
Ready for extension: Extend Writing
Invite students to write a second sentence explaining how one top source supports the innovator’s visibility, recognition, or representation in history.
Check for Understanding
Provide students with a confidence continuum (i.e., 1–5). As needed, model how to demonstrate a level of confidence using the continuum.
Check for Understanding
Reflect on your ability to identify relevant sources using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in identifying the most relevant sources for your inquiry questions?
Part A: Which Sources Answer the Question? (W.6.8)
Students will compare sources to determine which ones directly answer their inquiry questions and which ones are only loosely connected to their research question.
Part B: Build Your Final Short List (W.6.7)
Students will prioritize their two to three most relevant and useful sources and record them in their Research Notes graphic organizer.

This section assesses students’ ability to justify source selection using clear reasoning about relevance and centrality. Students reflect on how well their chosen sources directly answer their inquiry questions and support their understanding of an innovator’s contribution. Emphasize that strong researchers can explain not only why a source is useful, but why it is more relevant than other options by referencing specific details, sections, or features within the source. By the end of this section, students should be able to compare sources and clearly articulate why one belongs at the top of their research list.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
In two to three sentences, name your most relevant source and explain why it belongs at the top of your list. Compare it to one less central source and explain what makes the difference.
Ask:
What makes your top source more relevant than another source you found?

My top source is the science article because it directly answers my question about the innovator’s contribution. While another source relates to the same person, it mostly gives background facts and is less central to my research. The science article is more relevant because it specifically explains the work I need to describe in my final project.
Optional Sentence Starter:
“This source is most relevant because ___. While another source ___, this one ___.”
Students will formatively assess whether they can justify why one source is central to their research and another is less relevant.
Instruct students to review the two or three sources they recorded in the left column of the middle rows of their
Research Notes
graphic organizer. They should take notes in their
Journal
on the following prompt:
Mark one section that directly answers your inquiry question. Then, write one sentence naming that section and one sentence explaining why that detail is central to your research.

standards.description: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.

Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the credibility of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.
Analyze the use of text features (e.g., graphics, headers, captions) in popular media.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language resources to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the specific language used to present ideas and claims that are well supported and distinguishing them from those that are not), with light support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and arguments with detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the precise vocabulary used to present evidence, or the phrasing used to signal a shift in meaning), with substantial support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., showing the clarity of the phrasing used to present an argument), with moderate support.

Use various verb types (e.g., doing, saying being/having, thinking/feeling, reporting), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive, perfect) appropriate to the task, text type, and discipline (e.g., the present perfect to describe previously made claims or conclusions) on a variety of topics.

Use a variety of verb types (e.g., doing, saying, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive) appropriate to the text type and discipline (e.g., simple past and past progressive for recounting an experience) on familiar topics.

Use various verb types (e.g., doing, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling, reporting), tenses (e.g., present, past, future, simple, progressive, perfect) appropriate to the task, text type, and discipline (e.g., simple present for literary analysis) on an increasing variety of topics.

vocabulary.definition: the most important idea in a text or source
information that gives clear, exact details about a topic instead of being general
information that clearly answers or connects to your research question without needing a lot of guessing
basic information that helps you understand the topic but may not directly answer the research question
directly connected to the question or task
how directly something connects to the question or task
a one-sided point of view that can affect how information is presented
leaving something out because it does not fit the purpose
how people or groups are shown or included
how easily a person or contribution is seen or recognized
a small or less important piece of information that is related to the topic but not necessary for answering the research question
being left out by rules, systems, or patterns in society

content.text: Why were some contributions overlooked in historical accounts, and how can research help us build a fuller record?
